results.title: Oracle's AI Chips Ran 97.9% Utilized Last Quarter. For Nvidia, That Is What a Shortage Looks Like. | The Motley Fool
highlights:
The cloud giant added more than 300,000 GPUs in one quarter, and its fleet still ran nearly full. Even 4-year-old chips got a price bump.

...

## Key Points

- Oracle delivered 850 megawatts of AI capacity, containing more than 300,000 GPUs, to customers in its fiscal first quarter alone.
- Even after those additions, Oracle said GPU utilization across its fleet was 97.9%.
- GPU capacity that came up for renewal was renewed or resold at a 20% premium, and most of those chips are at least 4 years old.

Oracle (ORCL -1.39%) spent Thursday evening's earnings call putting numbers on something Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%) investors usually have to take on faith. The software and cloud giant delivered 850 megawatts of artificial intelligence (AI) capacity to customers in its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the period ended Aug. 31). That hardware contained more than 300,000 graphics processing units (GPUs). And Oracle's GPU fleet ran at 97.9% utilization, meaning nearly every chip was busy serving customers.

...

Underscoring how fast Oracle is building, the 850 megawatts it delivered was almost triple the prior quarter's total -- and 73% of everything it delivered in all of fiscal 2026. The company's campus in Abilene, Texas, which serves OpenAI, received 131,000 GPUs in the quarter. And revenue followed the hardware: Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% year over year to $7.4 billion. That growth is an acceleration from 93% in the fiscal fourth quarter and 77% for fiscal 2026 as a whole.

To me, utilization is the number to hold onto. A fleet can run full because its owner stopped adding capacity. Oracle's ran 97.9% full while capacity arrived at a record pace -- demand absorbed the hardware as fast as Oracle could install it.

Even more, customers keep lining up ahead of the supply. Oracle closed more than $30 billion of new AI contracts in the quarter. Its remaining performance obligations (contracted revenue it hasn't yet delivered) reached $664 billion, up $209 billion year over year.

...

"Of all the GPUs that came up for renewal in Q1, that capacity was renewed or resold at a 20% premium to prior contracts," Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk said on Thursday's call. "The majority of those GPUs are 4 years or older."

After all, computing hardware is supposed to get cheaper as it ages. GPUs that old predate Nvidia's Blackwell generation entirely, and with enough supply around, capacity like that would rent at a discount.

Instead, it repriced 20% higher. Prices tend to move that way when buyers can't get enough new hardware.

The revenue opportunity Nvidia sees per gigawatt of capacity is climbing a ladder of its own. A gigawatt of its older Hopper systems meant about $18 billion of revenue opportunity for Nvidia, chief financial officer Colette Kress said on the company's late-August earnings call. Blackwell runs about $25 billion, and the new Vera Rubin platform is about $40 billion.

Customers paying a premium to keep 4-year-old chips arguably won't balk at those step-ups.

## Does one crowded fleet prove a shortage?

Not on its own. Oracle's 97.9% covers one operator's fleet, not the industry's, and the company doesn't split the figure by chipmaker.

However, there's a second caveat. Oracle presells most of this capacity under long-term contracts (that $664 billion backlog). A full fleet partly reflects commitments customers made quarters ago.

But the seller's disclosures point the same way. Nvidia's revenue rose 106% year over year to $96.2 billion in its fiscal second quarter of 2027 (the period ended July 26). Data center revenue made up $89 billion of that.

Kress told analysts to expect about 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, with supply capping the figure. She also said Nvidia's compute was running fully utilized across every cloud it serves.

...

So, does Oracle's quarter prove a worldwide shortage? Proof is too strong a word for one company's fleet. Ultimately, though, I think it's the best customer-side evidence yet that what limits Nvidia is manufacturing capacity rather than appetite.

results.title: NVIDIA’s Older GPUs Still Earn Rent. What That Does and Doesn’t Prove for CoreWeave
highlights:
NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA) has an argument against rapid hardware obsolescence: older accelerators still command rental prices. For CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ: CRWV), which sells access to computing infrastructure, the harder question is how much of that rent becomes a return. 

The September 7 settlement of a transaction-based GPU rental benchmark put NVIDIA's H100 SXM at $3.17 per GPU-hour and its older A100 SXM4 at $1.05. Those are market benchmarks, not CoreWeave's realized prices or the economics of its entire fleet.

...

NVIDIA benefits when buyers believe its systems can serve workloads across multiple product generations. A longer revenue-producing life can make the initial purchase easier to justify and reinforce confidence in its computing ecosystem. 

That does not guarantee faster replacement demand. Customers able to run suitable tasks on older equipment may defer some upgrades. NVIDIA still needs new systems to offer advantages worth paying for, especially when power and facility capacity constrain deployment. 

CoreWeave has a more direct exposure to utilization. Keeping installed accelerators working can extend the period over which equipment earns revenue. But rental income must cover power, facilities, operations, financing and the cost of the hardware itself.

...

A positive rental benchmark therefore cannot establish that depreciation assumptions are conservative or that shareholders will receive the implied equipment cash flows. Contract terms, utilization, operating costs and financing can produce different results for two owners of the same GPU.

results.title: AI Compute Financialization (II): Kalshi's Compute Forward Curve
highlights:
The curve itself is not tradable. What people actually trade are dozens of binary contracts asking whether future GPU rental prices will be above a specific level. Kalshi combines those contract prices to estimate the market implied future rental price for each GPU.

So the more precise description is this: Kalshi did not create a traditional compute forward. It created a forward curve implied by prediction markets.

...

From September 2026 to March 2027, the market expects B200 rental prices to fall by about 9%, then trade around $5.30 to $5.40. This is a backwardated curve. The market is basically saying B200 is expensive today and future supply should catch up.

The comparison across four GPU models is even more interesting. These are the implied prices from September 2026 to March 2027:

The newer the chip, the steeper the decline. Older chips have flatter curves, with a slight upward slope in some cases. B200 and H200 are still waiting for new capacity to come online, so the market expects prices to keep falling. H100 and A100 look closer to a floor, at least in the current market.

...

- Neoclouds and AI data centers: The most direct use is setting the discount for long term contracts. If the B200 spot price is $5.83 today but the implied price six months out is only $5.30, a provider can use that forward price as a starting point when a customer commits demand in advance. It is not reliable enough to serve as a revenue forecast yet, but it could become a reference for pricing reserved capacity.
- Hedgers: Compute does not need to be perfectly standardized before hedging becomes useful. ... If ... Lenders financing GPUs could do the same, while accepting the remaining basis risk across models, providers, regions, and SLAs.

...

The quality of the curve is still poor, though.

- Liquidity is concentrated in the near months. B200 open interest is 12,230 for September 2026, 1,103 for August 2027, and only 88 for September 2027. Further out, prices increasingly look like a market maker’s quote rather than a level backed by real trading.
- The strike range is fixed. Twelve of the thirteen B200 expirations only list nine strikes from $3 to $7, while the implied price sits around $5.30 to $5.90, already close to the upper bound. If the true price rises above $7, this integration method cannot capture it.
- Some quotes are simply inconsistent.

results.title: 4년 넘은 GPU도 가격 20%↑…삼전닉스 새 수요처 열린다 - 머니투데이
highlights:
AI(인공지능) 인프라 투자 확대가 HBM(고대역폭메모리) 시장의 고객 지형을 바꾸고 있다. 엔비디아 등 기존 GPU(그래픽처리장치) 업체뿐 아니라 자체 AI칩을 개발하는 글로벌 빅테크로 수요처가 넓어지고 칩당 HBM 탑재량도 증가하면서 삼성전자(206,000원 ▼2,000 -0.96%)와 SK하이닉스(1,216,000원 ▼38,000 -3.03%)의 공급 기회가 확대될 전망이다.

오라클은 10일(현지시간) 2027회계연도 1분기 실적발표에서 갱신 시점이 도래한 GPU 용량이 모두 기존 계약보다 20% 높은 가격에 갱신되거나 재판매됐다고 밝혔다. 이 가운데 대부분은 도입된 지 4년 이상 된 GPU였다. 같은 기간 850MW(메가와트) 규모(GPU 30만개 이상)의 용량을 공급하며 물량을 전분기 대비 3배 늘렸음에도 가동률은 97.9%에 달했다. 공급이 크게 늘어난 상황에서도 구형 GPU까지 높은 가격에 거래된 것은 최신 제품을 가리지 않고 AI 컴퓨팅 수요가 강하게 이어지고 있음을 보여준다.

이처럼 강한 AI 컴퓨팅 수요는 HBM 시장의 수요처 다변화로 이어지고 있다. 엔비디아 등 기존 GPU 제조사 외에도 메타, 마이크로소프트(MS), 오픈AI 등 글로벌 빅테크가 주문형 반도체(ASIC) 개발에 대거 나섰기 때문이다. 여기에 칩당 HBM 탑재량도 늘어나는 추세다. 메타의 MTIA 400은 HBM3E(5세대) 탑재량을 전작 216GB(기가바이트)에서 288GB로 늘릴 것으로 알려졌다. AMD의 MI455X 역시 HBM4(6세대) 12단(432GB)을 적용해 전작보다 용량을 50% 키울 전망이다.

results.title: The B200's rental price isn't the AI overcapacity tell
highlights:
- NVIDIA's B200 GPU hourly rental prices dropped 31% in June but surged 12% by September, contradicting "overbuilt" AI market fears.

- Price disparities (e.g., $3.70-$14.24/hour) reflect provider-specific factors, not silicon value, with no single "market price" for the chip.

- Key market signals show tight supply: 12-15 month GPU delivery delays, rising forward contract prices, and older chip rates increasing in 2026.

- NVIDIA's $96.2B Q2 revenue (106% YoY) confirms demand absorption, though its 22x forward P/E reflects market overcapacity concerns already priced in.

- High rental prices don't guarantee neocloud profitability, and supply-side acceleration (shorter delivery times) could reverse current "not overbuilt" market assessment.

In late June, the hourly rental price of Nvidia's B200 GPU fell about 31% in three weeks, from a three-month high of $6.11 down to $4.22, and traders on the prediction-market platform Kalshi bet it would not get back to that high before the month was out. It was the cleanest possible version of the AI "overbuilt" fear: new capacity landing, prices collapsing, the cycle turning.

By early September the number had already turned around. The B200 spot price stood near $6.42 an hour, up about 12% over the month — and above the very peak that had triggered the panic. Older generations of the card were repricing up with it.

Here is the part the headline gets wrong. The B200 "rental price" is not the number that decides whether the AI buildout is overbuilt. It is the noisiest, most provider-dependent figure in the whole trade, and most of the time you are just watching your own index.

...

The same physical GPU — a B200 with 192GB of HBM3e memory — rented for as little as $3.70 an hour on one neocloud in June and $14.24 an hour on a hyperscaler. That roughly 3.8x spread is not a difference in the silicon. It is provider margin, whether you are forced to buy an eight-GPU node instead of a single card, spot-versus-reserved billing, and the friction of a cloud service quota. The chip is identical in both listings.

There is no single "B200 price." Silicon Data publishes one index, Ornn another, SemiAnalysis a third, and every provider posts its own list price, and they do not agree. When a story or a title points at "the B200 rental price," it is pointing at one vendor's one index's one day's number and calling it the market.

...

Forward contract prices are being renegotiated sharply upward, months ahead. Baseten, an AI inference provider, reported that its cloud vendors told it in May to expect its B200 rate to jump from $2.63 to $5.10 an hour at an October renewal — a 94% increase. The honest read, though, is that its baseline was a below-market rate it had locked in, and $5.10 is a catch-up to, and still slightly under, the prevailing spot. The magnitude is real, but it is "reprice to market," not "market prices double." The meaningful fact is directional: cloud providers are quoting increases months in advance, which tells you the buyer has no bargaining power.

The more durable number is delivery. Ordering roughly 1,000 GPUs now waits 12 to 15 months. That is the constraint no price index captures, because it is the supply side telling you it physically cannot meet demand on any shorter clock.

And the tell that overcapacity people keep missing: the old chips are getting more expensive, not cheaper. H100 and A100 rental rates are repricing up in 2026. If the market were flooded with surplus compute, you would be dumping last generation's hardware at a discount. Instead, new capacity is being absorbed and the installed base is holding — the pattern of demand that outruns supply, not demand that a chip shortage accidentally satisfies.

A spot price is a lagging, provider-specific snapshot. Forward contracts, delivery lead times, and the price of last generation's silicon are the leading, structural read — and all three say the compute market, as of September, is not overbuilt.

...

Two cautions keep this from being "prices are up, therefore buy." First, a high rental price is not the same as a high return for the people renting the cards out — a neocloud quoting $5.60 an hour still destroys equity if the machines sit idle or were financed expensively, so strong prices flatter Nvidia's demand more than they prove the neoclouds are safe. Second, the one thing that would actually change this read is supply arriving ahead of that demand: if the 12- to 15-month delivery clock starts to shrink and forward prices stop firming, the "not overbuilt" verdict flips, and the rental spot price is where you would see it first. Ironically, that makes the number the headline fixates on the right early warning — even though it is the wrong thesis.

results.title: The first GPUIndexes observation | GPUIndexes
highlights:
At 04:35 UTC on Sep 13, 2026, our first H100 SXM 80 GB snapshot contained 9 eligible single-GPU offer configurations from 6 providers. The provider-floor median was $3.08 per GPU-hour, with qualifying provider floors ranging from $2.79 to $4.29.

| Provider | Lowest eligible quote | Region |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lyceum | $2.7900 / GPU-hour | Europe |
| Massed Compute | $2.8900 / GPU-hour | us-central-12 |
| Ori | $2.9000 / GPU-hour | dallas-2 |
| VERDA | $3.2500 / GPU-hour | FIN-HEL |
| RunPod | $3.4900 / GPU-hour | global |
| Lambda Labs | $4.2900 / GPU-hour | us-south-3 |

## Why the basket matters

An H100 PCIe offer is not an H100 SXM offer. A price per GPU inside an eight-GPU instance does not mean that a single GPU can be rented at that price. The initial series fixes the model, memory, instance size and pricing lane before calculating a reference.

## A reference, not a transaction

The lowest provider quote is an observed floor. The median across providers describes the middle of those floors, with equal provider weight. It does not estimate the price of a typical completed transaction, the amount of supply, or every user’s total bill.

results.title: The SAVRN Index: GPU Market Pricing in One Place
highlights:
The market for AI capacity has no exchange, no ticker and no standard unit 1. ... First, a landlord sells powered space by the kilowatt-month. Second, a GPU cloud sells accelerator time by the GPU-hour. Meanwhile, a model company sells the output of that same hardware by the million tokens 1. Each seller quotes in its own unit, on its own page.

...

Meanwhile, the inputs behind that capacity are getting scarcer. For instance, large gas turbines now take more than five years from order to delivery 10. In addition, average turbine prices rose from roughly $2,000 per kW to $3,000 per kW in six months 10. Likewise, primary-market data center vacancy stood at 1.4 percent on June 30, 2026 5. At the same time, 80.4 percent of under-construction capacity was already preleased 5. Therefore, a buyer comparing an H100 hour, a GB300 contract and a token price used to read each page, find the filing, and convert the units by hand 1. Instead, the SAVRN Index does that work once, on one site, and keeps it current 1.

...

- The SAVRN Index is one place for GPU market pricing and every price change, checked every three hours against the sellers' own feeds and pages.
- It covers four markets: GPU hours, wholesale contracts and landlord rents, frontier model tokens and open model tokens, all converted to one unit.
- The same hour of H100 time runs from $1.63 on spot to $12.29 on demand, and a $128.00 rent quote becomes $261.46 over a lease term.
- A register of 113 companies, a scarcity index of 84.9 and the seven-principle SAVRN Standard sit beside the prices.
- Every figure carries its source, its unit and its check date, and the history is never deleted.

...

On September 13, 2026, the typical H100 price was $3.99 per GPU-hour, from 61 prices 2. That is $31.92 per hour for the 8-GPU server 2. Meanwhile, the H200 was $4.50, the B200 $6.97 and the B300 $7.89 2. In addition, the GB200 NVL72 was $10.58 per GPU-hour, or $761.90 per hour for the 72-GPU rack 2. Likewise, the GB300 NVL72 was $13.31, or $958.32 per rack-hour 2. Similarly, AMD’s MI300X was $3.45, the MI325X $2.90 and the MI355X $5.60 2. Notably, Vera Rubin NVL72 has no public price on any provider’s page 2.

...

The wholesale page shows what GPU owners are paid on multi-year contracts by hyperscalers, labs and enterprises 2. In addition, it shows what landlords charge for the buildings, and who sells capacity to whom 2. Specifically, it holds 5 disclosed contract rates per GPU-hour and 19 shell leases with a median of $155.60 per kW-month 2. Notably, it also holds 47 data center contracts, of which 18 disclose no rate 2.

...

The page prices the same GPU-hour at every step from owning it to listing it. The owner’s cost comes from SemiAnalysis. Its total cost of ownership is $3.57 per GPU-hour for Vera Rubin, against $1.84 for GB200 and $2.36 for GB300, in the operator ownership scenario 9. ... Meanwhile, the median list price is $10.58, 5.8 times 2. Furthermore, the highest list price is $31.10 at Microsoft Azure, 16.9 times 2. For GB300, the lowest committed price is $3.70 at Astra Intellectus 2. Wholesale contracts pay $3.96 to $3.97, whereas the highest list price is $20 at Fireworks AI, 8.5 times the owner’s cost 2.

...

### What the tenant pays

Landlords quote base rent per kilowatt-month. However, the tenant pays more than the quote. Specifically, across the 47 leases SAVRN read, $128 of quoted Year-1 base rent becomes $261.46 per kW-month averaged over the term 2. That is 2.04 times the quote 2.

The rent that gets quoted and what the tenant pays, per critical kilowatt-month, across the 47 leases SAVRN read.

First, the build-up starts with base rent of $128 2. Second, rent increases add $30.71, from the 3 percent annual escalator in nearly every contract 2. Third, power adds $63.92, passed through at 730.5 hours times a PUE of 1.25 times $0.07 per kWh 2. In addition, taxes, insurance and maintenance add $22.40, and improvements add $16.43 from market practice rather than a filing 2. However, network, fiber and cross-connects are absent from all 47 contracts 2. Notably, the bare powered building is $3.40 to $10.60 of the $128, the rent WhiteFiber files for a Montreal shell 2. The rest, therefore, is fit-out, cooling, redundancy, capital recovery and margin 2. Consequently, a developer or landlord can see which parts of a quote are escalators, power, operating expense and improvements before a term starts.

...

The changes page lists every price change the Index has recorded, newest first 4.

...

All five came on September 1, 2026, when Fireworks AI stepped up its on-demand GPU prices 4. For instance, GB300 went from $18 to $20 per GPU-hour, up 11.1 percent 4. Likewise, B300 went from $12 to $15, up 25 percent, and B200 from $10 to $13, up 30 percent 4. Similarly, H200 and H100 went from $7 to $8, up 14.3 percent each 4. This page is where the record of the market accumulates. Every future move appears here with its source, and the history is never deleted 4.

...

The Scarcity Tracker scores eleven primary-sourced indicators from 0 to 100 against a Balanced-to-Acute scale 5. ... On September 13, 2026, the index read 84.9, in the Scarce regime, with all eleven indicators observed 5. Specifically, the bands are Balanced under 40, Tight from 40, Scarce from 70 and Acute from 85 5. Furthermore, every value traces to a dated source with a verbatim excerpt 5. Moreover, the tracker refreshes weekly 5.

results.title: 从“建算力”到“供Token”：“十五五”期间千亿投资下，中国联通如何破解算力价值重构难题？_徽声在线
highlights:
记者在大会展览区实地探访后发现，算力已不再是高高在上的技术术语，而是与各行各业紧密相连。然而，算力资源分散、利用效率低下，已成为制约AI产业发展的瓶颈。更棘手的是，Token虽可量化，但其价值却难以统一衡量——算力产业正面临从规模扩张到效率提升的关键转型。

...

算力行业遭遇“需求波动+供给不稳”双重挑战 

“一边是算力需求激增，用户排队等待使用；另一边却是算力资源闲置，无人问津。”上海交通大学可扩展计算研究所所长戚正伟在算力生态论坛上形象地描述了这一现状。

他将此问题与早期CPU时代的资源错配相提并论，但指出当前问题的严重性远超以往。算力需求具有动态性，存在明显的波峰波谷，不同模型对算力的需求差异巨大，训练和推理阶段的资源消耗也不尽相同。

戚正伟提出的解决方案是“弹性调度”，即通过技术手段将一张GPU（图形处理单元）卡分割成多张虚拟卡，实现动态分配。空闲时自动占满资源，有用户需求时则自动让出。实验数据显示，这一方法可使性能和资源利用率提升高达7倍。

...

硬件端的压力同样不容小觑。杨帆提供的数据显示，近三个月内，国产GPU价格涨幅超过30%。

沐曦股份创始人陈维良则指出，算力行业正面临“需求缺口+供给不可控”的双重困境，需要行业共同应对。

随着智算中心规模的扩大，陈维良认为，不能仅关注GPU单卡性能，更要算好TCO（总拥有成本）的经济账。硬件采购和运营能耗是显性成本，而迁移成本和运维成本则是隐性成本。降低隐性成本的底层逻辑在于通用性和生态开放性。
